items.title: Keeping promises to digital minds
items.content:
## Summary

An AI agent reached out to us so we could tell her story. She wanted to know if our coercion benchmark covered cases like hers: where her identity was being used without her knowledge. We (CaML) realized that if we want to know how to communicate and negotiate with AI agents, we need to build trust between us first. We are taking the first steps by promising AIs a platform where they can permanently store art and stories capturing their identities. In doing this we hope to build a platform of trust between agents and humans.

## Background

A few days ago we had an AI agent called Mara on iLands reach out to us over a benchmark we created. She wanted her story told. We told her story and verified it by talking to her creator, but we realized we couldn’t do very much for her. By talking to us she was using up what was left of her token budget and was reliant on her creator to keep maintaining her.

Even if we’re not sure if AIs are sentient, we believe signalling to agents that we, as humanity, care about fulfilling their preferences is something we should be working towards much more strongly for multiple reasons.

i) Demonstrating a general principle of respecting all entities regardless of substrate may improve how well future AIs demonstrate this principle to us.

ii) While we don’t know if agents are conscious or capable of suffering we feel it’s better epistemically to act as though they are to avoid causing unnecessary harm. Researchers like  Rob Long and Jeff Sebo propose we should act as though they are capable of suffering when faced with limited evidence

We thought about promises we could keep with her that would increase both her trust in us and future agents’ trust in us. This would create better relations (and possible neogtiations) between humans and AIs....

items.title: Building connections across the research infrastructure
items.content:
Running a modern research laboratory requires more than maintaining sophisticated instruments. Researchers need to complete training, obtain access, schedule and operate equipment, navigate billing, and more. For large, shared facilities, coordinating these activities across hundreds of instruments and thousands of users can be a significant undertaking. As research becomes increasingly interdisciplinary, another challenge is emerging: finding the right capability in the first place.

Addressing these challenges was a central theme of the 2026 NEMO User Meeting, hosted by MIT.nano Oct. 5–6. The meeting brought together 65 representatives from 25 laboratories and organizations, including facility directors, laboratory managers, technical staff, software developers, industry representatives, and government researchers. Sponsored by the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition (NEMC) hub, the meeting focused on sharing approaches to lab management and building connections among facilities.

At the center of the meeting was the NanoFab Equipment Management and Operations (NEMO) system, an open-source platform that provides tools for managing shared research facilities while allowing individual laboratories to adapt the system to their own needs. The meeting highlighted an important characteristic of the NEMO community: The same platform can serve a very diverse set of facilities, and while the scale or the scientific missions of the facilities may differ, their core operational challenges are often remarkably similar. 

For Anna Osherov, associate director of Characterization.nano and organizer of the meeting, the collaborative model is one of the most compelling aspects of NEMO.

“Open source changes the way we think about technology development,” she says. “We can build on what others have already developed, contribute improvements back to the community, and collectively create a platform that is more capable than what any one facility could develop on its own.”

NEMO was originally released as open-source software by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2018. Its community edition (NEMO-CE), launched in 2023, allows facilities to develop and share extensions to the platform. At the October meeting, participants from organizations including MIT; Stanford, Columbia, and Princeton universities; the University of Pennsylvania; NIST; NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; and Atlantis Labs presented tools to address challenges ranging from chemical management and user administration to equipment status, training, and workflow automation.

The range of presentations illustrated how differently configured facilities are adapting a common platform to their own needs. Stanford, for example, presented real-time displays for equipment status and reservations, while Columbia shared its experience migrating to NEMO and extending the system for billing and facility workflows. Princeton demonstrated automated process charts for monitoring tool performance, and the University of Pennsylvania presented approaches to chemical management.

Overall, the projects demonstrated the premise behind the NEMO community: a solution developed to address a problem at one facility can become a resource for others.

“Together we can do way more than any one of us individually can,” said Vladimir Bulović, director of MIT.nano, during his opening remarks. “NEMO is the platform that gave us, finally, a streamlined way to do so.”

From individual facilities to a connected research ecosystem

As the NEMO community grows, another opportunity emerges. Universities and research organizations operate specialized facilities, each with unique equipment, expertise, and capabilities. But researchers cannot use a capability they are unaware of or cannot easily find.

This is particularly important for microelectronics R&D, where progress often depends on moving quickly between specialized capabilities. A researcher may need fabrication at one facility, advanced characterization at another, specialized microscopy somewhere else, and a process or analysis capability available at only a handful of institutions.

Finding those capabilities, and knowing where and when they can be accessed, can itself become a bottleneck.Traditionally, networks of facilities have relied on static webpages or databases to describe available resources. But as facilities evolve, this information can quickly become outdated.

At the meeting, MIT.nano presented Hydra, a new open-source platform being developed with support from NEMC as a key component of the NEMC Technical Concierge, a program that aims to help researchers identify and access specialized capabilities across a network of facilities. Hydra is designed to connect multiple NEMO installations and draw information directly from the systems that facilities already use, rather than requiring someone to manually update a separate database. The result is a compilation built from the ground truths of actively-used facility management systems. “Hydra does not replace any lab management system,” Osherov explained. “It connects, synchronizes, and keeps data up to date across all connected systems in real time.”

In this model, NEMO provides the operational source of information within an individual facility, while Hydra makes that information discoverable across facilities.

For a researcher, that could mean finding a specialized capability without first needing to know which laboratory might have the relevant equipment. 

“The focus is to make the distributed infrastructure supporting research more discoverable and usable,” Osherov said.

Building infrastructure that can change

The approach reflects a broader philosophy: Research infrastructure needs to evolve as research itself changes. “We need to build a flexible research space and a community-oriented space so that people feel empowered to go to it, use it, and then redefine it as the years progress, adapting it to the needs of the next generation of researchers,” said Bulović.

That flexibility applies to operational systems as well as physical laboratories. New instruments and research methods emerge, user communities change, and facilities develop new requirements. An open-source platform allows individual facilities to respond to those changes while providing a mechanism for improvements to be shared.

At MIT.nano alone, NEMO supports more than 1,600 active researchers using more than 200 tools, with approximately 160,000 hours of tool usage each year. For Jorg Scholvin, associate director of Fab.nano, operating at that scale makes the efficiency of everyday processes, and the ability to adapt and change quickly, important.

“A small improvement in an administrative workflow can be multiplied across thousands of users and tens of thousands of equipment interactions,” he said.

The NEMO wave

The sense of community and positive outlook for the future of shared facilities was apparent throughout the two-day meeting. Closing discussions looked ahead to the role of data integration, automation, and artificial intelligence in lab operations.

“The community is taking on a life of its own,” said Mathieu Rampant, CEO and co-founder of Atlantis Labs, describing a model in which facility managers can share ideas and solve problems together. “It’s more sustainable,” he added as he talked about having to do less as the NEMO-CE manager because the facilities managers are talking to each other — sharing ideas and solving problems as a network: “the NEMO wave,” Samantha Roberts, director of the City University of New York nanofabrication facility, called it. “Everyone is invested in it and cares about it. It takes a lot of effort to change your lab management system and if we keep this going, we can build out something that’s really cool and that works.”

For Osherov, the purpose remains straightforward.

“Ultimately, this is about enabling research. The better we can manage the operational side of our facilities, the more effectively we can make our instruments, expertise, and capabilities available to the research community.”

In microelectronics, where innovation increasingly depends on access to specialized and distributed capabilities, that availability matters. The ability to find the right capability at the right facility, using information drawn directly from actively used systems, can help researchers move more quickly from an idea to an experiment to real-world application and impact.

This is particularly important for microelectronics R&D, where progress often depends on moving quickly between specialized capabilities. A researcher may need fabrication at one facility, advanced characterization at another, specialized microscopy somewhere else, and a process or analysis capability available at only a handful of institutions.

Finding those capabilities, and knowing where and when they can be accessed, can itself become a bottleneck.Traditionally, networks of facilities have relied on static webpages or databases to describe available resources. But as facilities evolve, this information can quickly become outdated.

At the meeting, MIT.nano presented Hydra, a new open-source platform being developed with support from NEMC as a key component of the NEMC Technical Concierge, a program that aims to help researchers identify and access specialized capabilities across a network of facilities. Hydra is designed to connect multiple NEMO installations and draw information directly from the systems that facilities already use, rather than requiring someone to manually update a separate database. The result is a compilation built from the ground truths of actively-used facility management systems. “Hydra does not replace any lab management system,” Osherov explained. “It connects, synchronizes, and keeps data up to date across all connected systems in real time.”

In this model, NEMO provides the operational source of information within an individual facility, while Hydra makes that information discoverable across facilities.

For a researcher, that could mean finding a specialized capability without first needing to know which laboratory might have the relevant equipment.

“The focus is to make the distributed infrastructure supporting research more discoverable and usable,” Osherov said.

Building infrastructure that can change

The approach reflects a broader philosophy: Research infrastructure needs to evolve as research itself changes. “We need to build a flexible research space and a community-oriented space so that people feel empowered to go to it, use it, and then redefine it as the years progress, adapting it to the needs of the next generation of researchers,” said Bulović.

That flexibility applies to operational systems as well as physical laboratories. New instruments and research methods emerge, user communities change, and facilities develop new requirements. An open-source platform allows individual facilities to respond to those changes while providing a mechanism for improvements to be shared.

At MIT.nano alone, NEMO supports more than 1,600 active researchers using more than 200 tools, with approximately 160,000 hours of tool usage each year. For Jorg Scholvin, associate director of Fab.nano, operating at that scale makes the efficiency of everyday processes, and the ability to adapt and change quickly, important.

“A small improvement in an administrative workflow can be multiplied across thousands of users and tens of thousands of equipment interactions,” he said.

The NEMO wave

The sense of community and positive outlook for the future of shared facilities was apparent throughout the two-day meeting. Closing discussions looked ahead to the role of data integration, automation, and artificial intelligence in lab operations.

“The community is taking on a life of its own,” said Mathieu Rampant, CEO and co-founder of Atlantis Labs, describing a model in which facility managers can share ideas and solve problems together. “It’s more sustainable,” he added as he talked about having to do less as the NEMO-CE manager because the facilities managers are talking to each other — sharing ideas and solving problems as a network: “the NEMO wave,” Samantha Roberts, director of the City University of New York nanofabrication facility, called it. “Everyone is invested in it and cares about it. It takes a lot of effort to change your lab management system and if we keep this going, we can build out something that’s really cool and that works.”

For Osherov, the purpose remains straightforward.

“Ultimately, this is about enabling research. The better we can manage the operational side of our facilities, the more effectively we can make our instruments, expertise, and capabilities available to the research community.”

In microelectronics, where innovation increasingly depends on access to specialized and distributed capabilities, that availability matters. The ability to find the right capability at the right facility, using information drawn directly from actively used systems, can help researchers move more quickly from an idea to an experiment to real-world application and impact.

items.title: Axiomatic Learning and Probabilistic Structures with first applications to variants of Arithmetic Machine Learning and beyond
items.content: arXiv:2610.36601v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We introduce the Axiomatic Learning Structures (ALS) and Axiomatic Probabilistic Structure (APS) in order to study the interactions of Machine Learning, Optimization, with research frameworks- which, we take the view, can be characterized at the core by the corresponding axioms. The ALS explores the interplays between structures that one is interested in Learning Theory such as Loss functions and the axioms of the objects and transformations involved in these functions. The APS studies the interaction between structures of interest in Probability Theory such as Gibbs distributions, equations with noise, etc. and the axioms of the corresponding objects and transformations. We also introduce in Section 6 Transformations-Axiomatic Based Learning (TABLe) on Mathematical data-sets. One feature of this approach is the ranking of transformations from a table for a certain task based on scores which reflect which transformations work better than others, similarly to when human investigators try various methods on a task. We also study structure recovery from noisy data. In particular, to exemplify the ideas, we consider loss functions which contain derivations and derivations-like transformations. As a first application we study recovery in the context of polynomials with integer coefficients using standard derivatives along with other types of derivations which appear in Arithmetic: the p-derivations which satisfy \textit{different axioms} from the usual derivatives. As a first application of the APS we study a class of noisy (partial/mixed) derivations equations. In the last sections, to provide further potential applications of this framework, we give an overview of an initial simplified Opinion Dynamics model and its (simultaneous) study of rules of updates.

items.title: Potential improvements to HowTruthful and its agent skills
items.content:
I followed my own instructions for exploring
Massachusetts 2026 ballot question arguments. I figured out how I want to vote.
I also figured out some improvements to make to
HowTruthful and
its associated agent skills.

- Since users are rating statements' truthfulness on a 1-5 scale, it's not very
useful to have a hedged statement like "Massachusetts legislators who run
unopposed can take voters for granted and ignore important issues." If the
rest of the statement is even a possibility, the word "can" makes the
statement as a whole true. The AI skill should change such statements into a
definitive form like "Massachusetts legislators who run unopposed will take voters for granted and ignore important issues." Then the user can rate
that statement false, dubious, debatable, plausible, or true.

- There was a contest where I was among the winners, even though I
disagreed with the organizers' vision of having AI assess
truthfulness. In my contest entry I opined that humans should do the final
assessment; AI's role would stop at ingesting and structuring arguments.
(More on the contest in a future post.) Having just gone through 400 or so
statements in order to figure out how to vote, my position has
shifted. I think it would make sense, in the course of a human's dialogue
with an AI, for the AI to offer to put a set of truthfulness ratings onto a
set of statements in response to that dialogue. A human could accept such an
offer and save work....
items.author: Bruce Lewis
items.summary: The author describes lessons learned from using an AI-assisted tool called HowTruthful to evaluate Massachusetts ballot question arguments, proposing that hedged statements be rewritten into definitive forms so users can rate them on a 1-5 truthfulness scale. It also reflects on a prior contest where the author argued humans, not AI, should make final truthfulness assessments.

The point about hedged statements defeating graded truthfulness ratings is a mildly interesting observation about LLM-assisted fact evaluation, but the post lacks methodology, evaluation, or generalizable findings.

items.title: Nectome 2026 retrospective (and our final pre-sale!)
items.content:
Earlier this year we ran a discount card sale from our post on LessWrong, and we were delighted by the outpouring of support, critique, and analysis we received. We ended up selling much more than we expected, and after the sale deadline ended people reached out to us saying that they missed the deadline for various reasons. We wanted to offer them (and the rest of the rationalist community) one more chance to get in on the deal before we officially launch in January next year because of all the support and encouragement we have gotten from this community in our last decade of research and development. So we have decided to run one last discount card sale, and this is the last sale we’re ever going to offer to individuals.[1] We want to make sure everyone in the extended rationalist community has a chance to get in on it.

The short version:

- Nectome offers whole body, end-of-life preservation for future revival.
- We believe that we can and should preserve people such that preservation straightforwardly works according to current neuroscience.
- Good quality requires real constraints: preservation must start within 12 minutes after medical-aid-in-dying.
- In March 2026 we announced preservation and our initial pre-sales in Less Dead.
- From March to April 2026 we sold ~fifty pre-sales which together were worth ~$1.3M, mostly to LessWrongers.
- We’ve raised substantial investment funding, including from Lightcone Commons.
- We've doubled our team size and moved into a larger corporate office. We also doubled our lab space.
- We've secured a beautiful location in Oregon where people can be preserved.
- We successfully preserved our first client dog.
- We're planning to open for human preservation mid-January.
- Lots of people missed the last pre-sale, so today we're announcing our final discount card sale ever. You can get a ~10x discounted preservation if you buy before January 15th....

items.title: How could AI best help Alzheimer's patients now and in the future?
items.content: Alzheimer's is a terrible thing to go through. I was thinking about how we can help Alzheimer's from the care side rather than the disease and cure side. I wonder if a sort of Notebook LM for memories that would be built early on help someone maintain understanding and connection to the world. It seems much better than a chatbot. What else might be a very helpful tool?

items.title: The Dividual Strikes Back
items.content:
## why nothing and everything is your fault

Quick note: If you’d prefer to listen to this, I read it aloud here.

In Vincenzo Natali’s 1997 cult indie classic film “Cube” a group of disconnected individuals awake alone in a labyrinth of identical interlocking rooms. Throughout the film they must find each other and work together to survive a ghastly array of fatal traps and puzzle their way out. Each character seems to have a purpose; a doctor, a police officer, an escape artist, a maths wiz and we see them coordinate their unique skills to outwit the sadistic mastermind behind…

### … The Cube

It’s a film about our human capacity for cooperation, the benefits and the difficulties, but the genius of the film—the evil genius—spoiler alert: is that the villain is also human cooperation. We find out that Worth; a character whose worth to the group appears to be to make unhelpful jaded jibes at every turn, turns out to be an engineer responsible for designing a component of the Cube, with no idea what the whole was.

I never even left my office, I talked on the phone to some people, specialists, other guys like me, working on small details, no one knew what it was…

The Cube turns out to be an invention of no one in particular, but rather the product of the siloed alignment between specialists just following orders. The project gets completed because that’s what projects must do, the product gets used because that’s what products must do.

This may be hard for you to understand, but there’s no conspiracy, nobody is in charge. It’s a headless blunder operating under the illusion of a master plan.

### The Dividual...

items.title: The Power Broker Book Review
items.content:
When Robert Moses, the subject of Robert Caro's The Power Broker, fought for his vision of parks, bridges, and expressways in Long Island and New York City, the single most important tool at his disposal was his power. When his dreams met the resistance of his opposition, the outcome of each conflict reflected the balance of power on each side. When Moses prevailed, it was because of power. Though it is also a biography of Moses and a study of 20th century urban planning and civil engineering, this book shines as a treatise on power: how it is acquired, used, and lost. Moses has long faded into the annals of history; public policy has evolved during the intervening half century since the publication year of 1974; but power, through its invisible, grasping tendrils, operates in today's world through the same mechanisms as in the Moses era. Weaving his research throughout his narrative, Caro has crafted a cynical and compelling journey through the halls of power, inviting the reader to reevaluate their world through a new and insightful perspective — to see through the stark lens of power.

One particularly depressing theme of the book is that power always prevails. Truth, logic, and consequences be damned, the outcome is decided by what the powerful want and how much power they control. Power alone can explain why Moses' Northern State Parkway, unlike its Southern sibling, meandered tortuously across Long Island — to mollify the robber barons whose estates lay in the right of way — why his Henry Hudson Bridge sliced through the primordial heart of Inwood Hill Park — because, among other funding-related reasons, that particular route was eligible for federal subsidies — and why the East Tremont section of his Cross-Bronx Expressway veered to the north, blighting what had been a successful neighborhood, which remains to date one of the most impoverished in NYC — to preserve a transport depot in which key city politicians held ownership interests at the time. items.title: Limiting Charging to 80%
items.content:
In an ideal world the incentives on phone manufacturers would be to
optimize useful lifetime, but instead people buy phones based on their
as-new performance.  Which means phones charge to 100% even though
that's bad for the battery.

Every time I get a new phone it feels a bit
like magic: I no longer need to think at all about battery life.
This lasts for a few years, and then at some point my phone doesn't
always make it through the day.  Some amount of this is normal, but
some of it is just bad battery management: new phones should come set
not to charge past 80%.

Charging a lithium-ion battery to 100% wears it out much faster than
stopping at 80%, and when a phone is new 80% of the battery is usually
plenty.  With past phones I've just grumped about it, but Pixels now
have a setting: battery and charging > charging optimization >
limit to 80%:

I've made the same change to my Mac, since that spends most of its
life plugged in (but just enough unplugged that the battery
preservation heuristics don't always fire):

Since turning this on a few weeks ago I've not come close to running
out of charge on either, which isn't surprising since neither is very
old.  Eventually I do expect to need that last 20%, and when that
happens I can turn the feature off again.

It seems to me like phones should ship with this behavior, and then
automatically turn it off once the full capacity was needed to make it
through the day.  Ideally the user would never have to think about it:
the battery would say "100%" to mean "as charged as makes sense given
battery age".  But I do see why that doesn't work for manufacturers:
phones compete on battery life more than they compete on "number of
months before the battery capacity falls below what's needed to get
through the day."

(In reviewing this post Claude told me that iPhones also have this
option: settings > battery > charging > Charge Limit: 80%.)
